domain_entities.name: AuditLog
attributes: id: string (UUID, generated by the repository via randomUUID — GP-007)
actorId: string (the employee who performed the action; never the viewer)
action: AuditAction (CREATE | UPDATE | DELETE | APPROVE | REJECT | CANCEL)
entityType: string (the entity discriminator; for a leave request the canonical value is exactly 'leave_request')
entityId: string (the id of the entity the action was performed on — for a GP-008 reversal this is the ORIGINAL request id, not the reversal row's id)
beforeState: unknown | null (the entity snapshot before the action; null on CREATE)
afterState: unknown | null (the entity snapshot after the action)
occurredAt: Date (stamped by the repository at insert; the sole ordering key of a trail)
domain_entities.purpose: The immutable, append-only record of one state-changing operation. Existing entity (Phase 3), unchanged in shape; this feature makes it READABLE by entity rather than only by its own id, which is what turns a write-only log into a trail.
lifecycle_states: RECORDED — the only state. Terminal and immutable: an entry is never updated, deleted, or re-recorded. Reached exactly once, at insert, inside the unit of work of the operation it describes.

domain_entities.name: AuditTrail
attributes: entityType: string (the discriminator the trail was queried by; 'leave_request' for this feature)
entityId: string (the entity whose trail this is)
entries: AuditLog[] (the matching entries, ordered by occurredAt ASCENDING — oldest first; may be empty)
entryCount: number (entries.length; 0 is a valid, non-error trail)
domain_entities.purpose: The read model of one entity's audit history: the ordered set of AuditLog entries for a single (entityType, entityId) pair. It is a projection, not a persisted entity — it has no id, no table, and no lifecycle of its own beyond EMPTY vs POPULATED. It exists so the domain has a name for 'the history of X' that is distinct from 'one audit entry', and so the empty case is a first-class outcome rather than an absence.
lifecycle_states: EMPTY — the entity exists and is visible to the caller, but no AuditLog row matches (entityType, entityId). A normal, successful outcome, never an error and never a 404.
POPULATED — one or more matching entries, ordered oldest first. The only other state; there is no partial or error state, because a failed read throws rather than producing a trail.

business_rules: A trail is identified by the PAIR (entityType, entityId), never by entityId alone. entityType is the exact, case-sensitive discriminator string written at record time; for a leave request it is exactly 'leave_request' (the literal already used by every leave.service.ts audit write). A query that omits entityType, or matches it case-insensitively or by prefix, is not a trail query. This is binding for every consumer of the entity query, not just the leave history endpoint. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever audit trail identity (entityType + entityId) appears, not only here]

A trail is ordered by occurredAt ASCENDING (oldest first) — the canonical order for every trail read, everywhere. occurredAt is the sole ordering key; no secondary key (id, action, actorId) may be used to re-order, and no consumer may reverse the order for display. The order is a property of the query, not of the caller, so a second trail consumer cannot legitimately ask for a different order. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever audit trail ordering appears, not only here]

occurredAt is NOT guaranteed unique: the repository stamps it with new Date() at insert, and two entries written in the same millisecond (e.g. a reversal's CANCEL entry and a sibling write in one unit of work) can collide. Ordering by occurredAt alone is therefore not a total order. The trail must be deterministic under ties: the entity query orders by occurredAt ASCENDING with a stable tie-break on id ASCENDING, so repeated reads of the same trail return the same sequence. A consumer must not assume two entries with equal occurredAt are interchangeable. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever audit trail ordering (ties) appears, not only here]

Who may see a leave request's history is EXACTLY who may see the leave request itself — the existing leave-module visibility rule (ADMIN sees all; a MANAGER sees their own plus their direct reports, one level only, not transitive; anyone else only their own), owned by the leave module and expressed in exactly one place (LeaveService.getById). The history read must establish visibility by calling the existing getById(actor, requestId) first and letting it throw; it must not re-derive, re-express, or branch on EmployeeRole anywhere else — including in the audit module, which must stay role-blind. Visibility is status-unrestricted and identical for the original APPROVED row and its CANCELLED reversal row. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever audit trail visibility (leave request history) appears, not only here]

A caller who may not see the leave request receives the SAME 404 (NotFoundError, code NOT_FOUND, byte-identical body) as a caller asking for a request that does not exist. Never 403, never 401, never an empty trail. The endpoint must not leak existence: an invisible request and a nonexistent request are indistinguishable in status, body, and timing class. This is the same contract GET /leaves/:id already honours, and the history endpoint inherits it by delegating to getById rather than by re-implementing a check. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever audit trail visibility (information hiding) appears, not only here]

An empty trail is a SUCCESS, not an error: when the request exists and is visible to the caller but no AuditLog row matches (entityType='leave_request', entityId=requestId), the outcome is a successful read of an EMPTY trail (200 with an empty array), never 404 and never an error. Emptiness is a property of the trail, not of the request — the request's existence and visibility are established independently, by getById, before the trail is read. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever audit trail emptiness appears, not only here]

A GP-008 reversal row (a leave_requests row with reversesRequestId non-null) has NO audit entries of its own: the CANCEL entry written when an APPROVED request is reversed carries entityId = the ORIGINAL request id, not the reversal row's id. Consequently GET /leaves/:reversalId/history legitimately returns an EMPTY trail (200, empty array) even though the reversal row exists and is visible. This is correct, not a bug: the reversal is an event in the ORIGINAL's history, and the reversal row is a terminal, inert artifact. A consumer must not 'fix' this by writing a second audit entry against the reversal row, and must not infer the reversal's provenance from the trail — provenance is reached via reversesRequestId. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever audit trail scope (GP-008 reversal) appears, not only here]

The trail is append-only and read-only. Reading a trail writes nothing: no audit entry is recorded for a history read (a read is not a state-changing operation, so GP-002 does not apply), no entity is mutated, and no transaction is opened. Conversely, no operation may update or delete an AuditLog entry — a correction is a new entry, never an edit. A trail read must never be the reason a row appears in audit_logs. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever audit trail immutability appears, not only here]

Every state-changing leave operation writes exactly one AuditLog entry against the request it changed, with entityType='leave_request' and entityId = the id of the row it changed — EXCEPT the GP-008 reversal, whose CANCEL entry targets the ORIGINAL id. The trail for a request is therefore the complete, ordered record of that request's lifecycle: CREATE (create), UPDATE (submit), APPROVE, REJECT, CANCEL. A state-changing operation that writes no entry, or writes two, is a GP-002 breach. This rule is what makes the trail trustworthy as history rather than a partial log. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever audit trail completeness (GP-002) appears, not only here]

A trail read returns ALL matching entries for the (entityType, entityId) pair — no limit, no offset, no date filter, no action filter, no truncation. Pagination and filtering of a trail are explicitly out of scope, so the entity query must not accept them and no consumer may assume a bounded result. A trail is a complete history or it is not a trail. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever audit trail read scope appears, not only here]

Each entry in a trail is projected as exactly { id, actorId, action, entityType, entityId, beforeState, afterState, occurredAt } — the full AuditLog shape, with beforeState/afterState passed through as the stored unknown|null value (never re-serialized, never redacted, never omitted when null). No field is added, renamed, or dropped, and no derived field (e.g. a human-readable action label) is introduced. The projection is the entity, not a summary of it. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever audit trail entry projection (wire shape) appears, not only here]
domain_notes:
## Domain slice — Audit trail for a single leave request

### Entities
- **AuditLog** (existing, unchanged shape): id, actorId, action, entityType, entityId, beforeState, afterState, occurredAt. This feature adds no field; it adds a *read path* by entity.
- **AuditTrail** (new, read model / projection — no table, no id, no persistence): entityType, entityId, entries: AuditLog[], entryCount. It is the domain's name for "the history of one entity", distinct from "one audit entry", and it makes the empty case a first-class outcome rather than an absence.

### Lifecycle states introduced (for architectureMdUpdate)
1. **AuditLog.RECORDED** — unchanged, restated for completeness. Terminal and immutable; reached exactly once at insert, inside the unit of work of the operation it describes.
2. **AuditTrail.EMPTY** — NEW. The entity exists and is visible to the caller, but no AuditLog row matches (entityType, entityId). A normal, successful outcome: 200 with an empty array, never 404, never an error.
3. **AuditTrail.POPULATED** — NEW. One or more matching entries, ordered oldest first. The only other state; there is no partial or error state, because a failed read throws rather than producing a trail.

No LeaveRequest, LeaveBalance, Notification, Employee, LeaveType or LeavePolicy lifecycle state is added, removed, or changed. LeaveRequest keeps DRAFT | SUBMITTED | APPROVED | REJECTED | CANCELLED; the GP-008 reversal row remains born-CANCELLED and terminal.

### Binding rules (all scope "broad" — none is a narrow assertion inside one check)
- Trail identity is the PAIR (entityType, entityId); entityType is the exact literal `'leave_request'`, matched case-sensitively.
- Trail order is occurredAt ASCENDING, everywhere, with a stable tie-break on id ASCENDING (occurredAt is not unique — the repository stamps `new Date()` at insert, so same-millisecond collisions are possible).
- Visibility is EXACTLY the leave module's existing rule, established by calling the existing `getById(actor, requestId)` and letting it throw. It must not be re-expressed anywhere, and the audit module must stay role-blind (HARNESS.json `ownedDecisions`: EmployeeRole is owned by `leave` and `web-leave`).
- An invisible request and a nonexistent request are indistinguishable: the same 404, never 403.
- An empty trail is a success, not an error.
- A GP-008 reversal row has NO trail of its own — its CANCEL entry carries the ORIGINAL request id — so a reversal row's history is legitimately empty.
- The trail is append-only and read-only: reading writes nothing (GP-002 does not apply to a read), and no entry is ever updated or deleted.
- Every state-changing leave operation writes exactly one entry against the row it changed, except the reversal (which targets the original). This is what makes the trail complete history rather than a partial log.
- A trail read returns ALL matching entries: no limit, offset, date filter, or action filter.
- Each entry is projected as exactly { id, actorId, action, entityType, entityId, beforeState, afterState, occurredAt } — the entity, not a summary.

### Concerns surfaced (not silently resolved)
- **The empty-trail case is reachable in production, not hypothetical.** `LeaveService.cancel`'s GP-008 branch writes its CANCEL entry with `entityId: request.id` (the ORIGINAL), so the reversal row's own trail is empty by construction. The feature's "empty history returns 200" requirement is therefore load-bearing for every reversal row, not just for a request whose audit writes failed. Recorded as an open question because the alternative (a second entry against the reversal row, or transparently returning the original's trail) is a real design choice with a backfill cost.
- **beforeState/afterState exposure.** The trail is visible to exactly the callers who may see the request, so it grants no new *entity* access — but it makes full before/after snapshots bulk-readable and additionally reveals the actorId of every actor who touched the request (e.g. an ADMIN's id on an approval). Recorded as an open question; the projection rule is binding feature-wide, so redaction must be decided now if wanted.
- **Ordering is not index-covered.** The existing `audit_logs` index is (entity_type, entity_id); it supports the filter but not the occurredAt ordering or the id tie-break. Correctness is unaffected, but the ordering rule is stated as a query property rather than left to the index. Flagged for the data architect.
- **No contradiction with docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.** The document already records `audit_logs` with an `(entity_type, entity_id)` index and the "same 404 for invisible and nonexistent" contract on `GET /leaves/:id`; this feature extends both rather than re-deciding them. The one genuinely new thing is that the audit module gains an entity-scoped read, which is a read path, not a new boundary — `audit` still depends only on shared foundations and still does not import `leave` or branch on EmployeeRole.

### Discovery caveat
The discovery pass for this task was truncated at its iteration cap and returned no findings; everything above was re-verified by reading `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/GOLDEN_PRINCIPLES.md`, `HARNESS.json`, `src/modules/audit/*`, `src/modules/leave/leave.model.ts`, `src/modules/leave/leave.service.ts` and `src/modules/leave/leave.routes.ts` directly.

open_questions.question: Should a GP-008 reversal row have a non-empty trail of its own? Today the reversal's CANCEL entry is written against the ORIGINAL request id, so GET /leaves/:reversalId/history returns an empty array for a row that plainly exists and was plainly created by an action. A UI rendering a reversal row's history shows nothing.
open_questions.impact: Determines whether the empty-trail case is a rare edge or the normal outcome for every reversal row, and whether a client can explain a reversal from the trail alone. Changing it later means backfilling or double-writing audit entries, which conflicts with the append-only rule.
candidate_options: Keep as-is (binding): the reversal is an event in the ORIGINAL's history; the reversal row's trail is legitimately empty and the client pairs rows via reversesRequestId
Write a second CANCEL entry against the reversal row's own id as well (two entries per reversal, one per row)
Have the history read for a reversal row transparently return the ORIGINAL's trail (the reversal row is a view onto the original's history)
Return 404 for a reversal row's history, treating a reversal as not independently addressable

open_questions.question: Does exposing beforeState/afterState verbatim on the trail widen data exposure beyond what GET /leaves/:id already grants? The trail is visible to exactly the same callers as the request, but it additionally reveals the actorId of every actor who acted on it (e.g. an ADMIN's id on an approval) and full before/after snapshots.
open_questions.impact: beforeState/afterState carry full entity snapshots (employeeId, dates, reason, approverId). If a manager may read a direct report's trail, they see the report's request snapshots — which they can already see via GET /leaves/:id, so the exposure is not new, but the trail makes it bulk-readable and includes the actorId of every actor who touched the request. If redaction is wanted, it must be decided now, because the projection rule is binding feature-wide.
candidate_options: Keep the full beforeState/afterState payloads verbatim (current binding rule) — the trail is the record, and a manager who may see the request may see its states
Redact beforeState/afterState for non-ADMIN callers, exposing only the metadata fields
Expose beforeState/afterState only for entries whose actorId is the caller or whose entity is the caller's own request
Add a separate, narrower 'summary' projection for non-ADMIN callers

open_questions.question: The existing audit_logs index is (entity_type, entity_id) — it does not cover the occurredAt ordering or the id tie-break. Is a covering index required, or is an in-memory sort acceptable for a trail read?
open_questions.impact: The existing (entity_type, entity_id) index supports the filter but not the ordering, so every trail read sorts in memory. This is a performance concern only, not a correctness one, but it is the reason the ordering rule must be stated as a query property rather than left to the index.
candidate_options: Leave the index as-is; accept the sort for now and revisit if trail reads become hot
Add a composite index on (entity_type, entity_id, occurred_at) — the data architect's call, recorded here as the domain's ordering requirement
Add (entity_type, entity_id, occurred_at, id) to make the tie-break index-covered
